beginner.headline: New Technology Changes Life on Farms
beginner.brief: New technology is changing how some farmers work. George McMaster started farming by milking eight cows. He now has 300 cows and watches them through a camera. The camera makes a short video of each cow every day. It can find changes before farmers can see them. One farmer says healthier cows give them more milk. Some cows use a milking machine when they want to. A faster internet connection helped one farmer open a farm shop. A farmer uses an app to help run his farm. In this app, each cow has a page with all her records in one place. The app's developer says farmers should make the decisions. He says the technology helps farmers see the right information at the right time.

intermediate.headline: AI Helps Farmers Care for Cows and Save Time
intermediate.brief: George McMaster began his farming career by milking eight cows and checking their health by eye. Today, he monitors a herd of 300 cows through an AI camera at his farm near Islandmagee. The camera's software identifies each cow, analyses a short daily video and highlights changes that people may not yet see. The farmer says the camera helps identify cows with walking problems earlier than daily observation alone. The farmer believes healthier cows produce more milk, bringing benefits for both animals and farmers. Cows enter a robotic milking machine whenever they choose, instead of being gathered at fixed times. Better broadband has allowed the farmer to open a farm shop that accepts electronic payments. The farmer has used the FarmDrive app to run his business for four years. The app lets him enter information immediately, instead of writing it down in both the cattle building and the office. It also allows him to prepare reports for inspections, including details about animal medicines and feed. Each cow can have a profile that keeps all her information together, with the option of adding a photo. The developer sees AI as an adviser that helps farmers find useful information and work more efficiently. He believes farmers should remain responsible for decisions, rather than letting AI make those decisions for them.

advanced.headline: How AI Is Changing Farming and Supporting Human Judgement
advanced.brief: George McMaster began his farming career milking eight cows and relying on visual judgement to detect health problems. He now watches a herd of 300 through an AI camera in the milking parlour at his farm near Islandmagee in County Antrim. The camera uses an algorithm, a set of computational rules, to identify individual cows, analyse daily footage and flag changes that may not yet be visible to a person. A farmer reports that the camera can identify lameness, or difficulty walking normally, earlier than ordinary daily checks had revealed it. A farmer also links healthier cattle with greater milk production and better animal welfare. In the robotic milking arrangement described, automation allows cows to enter and leave the machine when they choose, rather than being brought in at fixed times. For one farmer, obtaining high-speed broadband was a turning point that enabled him to open a farm shop accepting electronic payments. One farmer describes a lighter administrative burden, with information entered as work is done rather than written down both in the cattle house and in the office. A compliance section allows reports on medicines, feed and other farm information to be selected in preparation for inspections. Another stated priority is for AI to help reduce inputs, the resources farming uses, while increasing outputs, what it produces. Although one speaker is enthusiastic about the technology, he does not believe it will replace humans. One speaker explicitly rejects the prospect of AI taking over farmers' decision-making. One contributor argues that combining datasets could advance sustainability across its economic, environmental and social dimensions. Digitalisation is also presented as a way to help farmers meet their obligations while supplying good-quality, sustainable food.
